originalTitle: Far-right Republican accused of stiffing student debate champion of $8,000
summary: Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback calls failure to pay Briana Whatley money owed ‘an oversight’
content: A far-right Republican candidate in Florida’s governor’s race has been accused of stiffing a high school debate champion over the better part of $11,000 in scholarship money she won from a company he founded. Student Briana Whatley landed the awards as regional and national champion of Incubate Debate, a league-style competition set up by the candidate, James Fishback, to encourage youth to engage in political discourse. A recording posted to Substack by Fishback in May 2024 shows Whatley, now a second-year history student at Florida State University, accepting a $10,000 check for besting seven other finalists in the 2024 Incubate Debate national championship, adding to two $500 area awards she previously won. According to Florida Politics, Whatley is suing Fishback for not delivering $8,000 of the money that a letter from the company promised would be paid to her in full on the day she graduated high school in May last year. The filing names Incubate Foundation Inc, the parent of Incubate Debate, and Fishback, 31, who is challenging front-running US congressman Byron Donalds and Jay Collins, the lieutenant governor of Florida, for the Republican nomination for state governor in November. The candidates face off in an 18 August primary. Whatley’s lawsuit, seen by the Guardian, was filed in small claims court in Broward county, where both she and Fishback went to school. Among the allegations are that Incubate Debate initially failed to respond to emails asking where the money was, then tried to change the terms of how it would be paid to her. Fishback, it said, “personally evaded and defrauded Plaintiff by initially ignoring communications, later blaming a terminated employee for the written award terms, falsely claiming an unwritten ‘installment policy,’ and delaying payment for months”. The document said Fishback admitted he “totally dropped the ball on this one” in a November 2025 text asking her to resend her bank details, then in December paid only $3,000 via Zelle. In another text, Fishback allegedly claimed that the employee who sent the original award letter promising payment in full on graduation had been fired, and that installment payments had “always been the case”, despite no previous mention of it. The text exchanges indicate a previously cordial relationship between the pair, with Fishback calling Whatley “a star”, and the student thanking him for “wanting to make it right”. Whatley claims Fishback broke off communication five months ago after she questioned why a promised 1 February installment was not paid. She is suing for the outstanding $8,000 plus interest and costs, and a pretrial conference is scheduled for 9 September. Whatley, the lawsuit said, has “suffered severe financial injury and out-of-pocket damages” as a result of Fishback’s alleged failure to pay. In a brief emailed statement to the Guardian on Monday, Fishback said: “This was an oversight on my part. We are fixing it.” In a court ruling last week, Fishback survived a legal challenge by Collins to remove him from this month’s primary. A judge in Tallahassee ruled that Fishback had not violated a rule requiring a gubernatorial candidate to be a resident of the state for seven years prior to the election, even though he bought a condo in Washington DC in 2020 that he declared his primary residence, and voted there. The lawsuit over scholarships follows a May 2023 episode in which Fishback and Whatley appeared to be on the same page in their criticism of the National Speech and Debate Association (NSDA), a rival to Incubate Debate, over censorship. Fishback wrote an essay for The Free Press, then owned by Bari Weiss, the CBS news editor-in-chief, stating that the NSDA had become a “woke” organization “hijacked by left-wing politics” that was telling students what they could and could not talk about. Whatley, then a high school sophomore, told Fox News Digital that she was warned by the organization to refrain from bringing up then former president Donald Trump during debates because it would be “inappropriate”.
chineseTitle: 极右翼共和党人被指控向学生辩论冠军索取 8,000 美元
chineseSummary: 佛罗里达州州长候选人詹姆斯·菲什巴克 (James Fishback) 称未能向布莱恩娜·惠特利 (Briana Whatley) 支付欠款是“疏忽”
chineseContent: 佛罗里达州州长竞选中的一名极右翼共和党候选人被指控在高中辩论冠军的问题上与一名高中辩论冠军进行较量，后者从他创办的一家公司获得了 11,000 美元的奖学金。学生布莱恩娜·沃特利 (Briana Whatley) 荣获孵化辩论地区和全国冠军称号，这是一项由候选人詹姆斯·菲什巴克 (James Fishback) 发起的联盟式竞赛，旨在鼓励年轻人参与政治讨论。 Fishback 于 2024 年 5 月在 Substack 上发布的一段录音显示，现在是佛罗里达州立大学历史系二年级学生的 Whatley，在 2024 年 Incubate Debate 全国锦标赛中击败其他七名决赛选手后，接受了 10,000 美元的支票，这也是她之前赢得的两项 500 美元领域奖项的基础上。据《Florida Politics》报道，沃特利正在起诉菲什巴克，因为该公司在一封信中承诺，将在她去年 5 月高中毕业那天全额支付给她 8,000 美元的资金，而菲什巴克却没有兑现。文件中提到了 Incubate Debate 的母公司 Incubate Foundation Inc 和 31 岁的菲什巴克 (Fishback)，后者在 11 月份的共和党州长提名中挑战领先的美国国会议员拜伦·唐纳德 (Byron Donalds) 和佛罗里达州副州长杰伊·柯林斯 (Jay Collins)。两位候选人将在 8 月 18 日的初选中展开对决。 《卫报》看到，惠特利的诉讼是在布劳沃德县的小额索赔法院提起的，她和菲什巴克都在那里上学。其中一项指控是，Incubate Debate 最初没有回复询问这笔钱去向的电子邮件，然后试图改变向她支付这笔钱的条款。菲什巴克，它说，“个人逃避和欺骗了原告，最初忽视了沟通，后来将书面奖励条款归咎于一名被解雇的员工，错误地声称有不成文的‘分期付款政策’，并推迟了交付。”
whyItMatters: 这条信息属于全球新闻信号，适合用于观察外部环境、政策变化、地缘风险和市场情绪。
